title: Chapter 7.  The Sixth Schedule & Statehood Demand — Ladakh's Defining Current-Affairs Issue

blocks.content: This is the single most important current-affairs chapter in the entire Ladakh GS book. The demand for statehood and Sixth Schedule protection has dominated Ladakhi politics since 2019 and reached a violent, nationally reported crisis point in September 2025 — essential, high-probability exam material.
What is the Sixth Schedule, and Why Does Ladakh Want It?

The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, made under Article 244(2) and Article 275(1), provides for the administration of certain tribal areas through Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) with legislative, judicial and executive powers over specified local subjects (land, forests, agriculture, village administration, inheritance, marriage/divorce, and social customs, among others) — currently applicable ONLY to specified tribal areas of four North-Eastern states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

Ladakh's civil-society leadership (LAB and KDA, Chapter 6) argues that, following the 2019 removal of Article 35A's land/employment protections (which applied to Ladakh as part of erstwhile J&K, detailed in the companion J&K GS volume), the region — whose population is overwhelmingly tribal (predominantly Scheduled Tribe communities in both Leh and Kargil districts) — now lacks ANY comparable constitutional safeguard against land alienation, unregulated outside investment/settlement, and cultural/environmental disruption, given Ladakh's fragile high-altitude ecology and small population relative to the rest of India.

The demand for Sixth Schedule inclusion is thus explicitly framed as a request to extend an EXISTING constitutional mechanism (already used in the North-East) to a new region, rather than a request for an entirely new or unprecedented category of protection — though extending it to Ladakh would require a constitutional amendment, since the Schedule's coverage is not automatically extensible by executive action alone.

★ EXAM POINT: Sixth Schedule = Article 244(2)/275(1); CURRENTLY covers only Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram (sometimes remembered by the acronym 'ATMM'). Ladakh's inclusion would require a CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (Parliament, not just an executive order) — a frequently tested procedural fact distinguishing this demand from simpler administrative asks.

cells: An elected Legislative Assembly (proposed at approximately 30 members) and Council of Ministers, replacing the current LG-only administration
Extension of Autonomous District/Regional Council-style constitutional protection over land, resources and cultural/social customs
Separate Lok Sabha seats for Leh and Kargil

Currently Ladakh has only 1 combined Lok Sabha seat covering both districts; the demand seeks 2 separate seats, one for each district, to ensure distinct representation for Leh's Buddhist-majority and Kargil's Muslim-majority populations

A dedicated local public-service commission with a high (reportedly around 85%) reservation quota for Ladakhi domiciles in local government jobs, addressing concerns about job security given Ladakh's very small population and limited local employment base

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Ladakh currently has only 1 Lok Sabha seat covering BOTH Leh and Kargil districts jointly — the demand for 2 SEPARATE seats (one per district) is a distinct, specific ask worth remembering alongside the broader statehood/Sixth Schedule demands.

cells: Initial post-reorganisation period; growing civil-society mobilisation as the practical limitations of no-Assembly UT status became apparent; formation of LAB and KDA as advocacy platforms
Union Home Ministry forms the High-Powered Committee (HPC), chaired by a Minister of State, to negotiate directly with Ladakhi representatives on land, employment and cultural-protection concerns
Sonam Wangchuk leads the 'Delhi Chalo' padayatra (foot march) from Leh to Delhi, culminating at Raj Ghat on Gandhi Jayanti, drawing national attention to the Sixth Schedule demand
Wangchuk undertakes a 21-day 'climate fast' hunger strike in Leh (beginning 6 March 2025), joined by hundreds of others, later paused around the LAHDC election period
Violent clashes erupt in Leh during protests linked to the ongoing agitation; 4 protesters killed and nearly 100 injured after police firing; BJP offices in Leh set on fire
Sonam Wangchuk arrested under the National Security Act (NSA), which permits detention without trial for up to 12 months; his land allotment cancelled and FCRA licence revoked amid the crackdown
Union Home Ministry announces a judicial inquiry commission (headed by a retired Supreme Court judge) into the September violence, accepting one of the Ladakhi leaders' key demands

LAB and KDA jointly submit a detailed 29-page draft proposal to the Home Ministry, seeking full statehood (30-member Assembly), Sixth Schedule extension, and a general amnesty for Wangchuk and other arrested protesters

Wangchuk released from Jodhpur Central Jail after the Centre revokes the NSA charges against him, explicitly framed as an effort to build 'an environment of peace, stability and mutual trust' for renewed dialogue

Fresh rounds of HPC-led dialogue anticipated; Ladakhi leaders continue to describe statehood and Sixth Schedule protection as 'non-negotiable' twin demands, while remaining open to phased or sequenced approaches to achieving them

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The September 2025 Leh violence (4 deaths) and Sonam Wangchuk's subsequent NSA detention (26 Sept 2025 - 14 March 2026, released after charges were revoked) are THE defining current-affairs sequence for Ladakh as of 2026 — essential to know both the dates and the causal sequence (protests -> violence -> arrest -> release) for any current-affairs question on this UT.

items: The Union Government's response has generally emphasised ongoing dialogue through the High-Powered Committee, while expressing reservations about extending the FULL, direct Sixth Schedule model (citing its design for the specific North-Eastern context) and reportedly exploring alternative or hybrid protective mechanisms (including discussion of Article 371-style special provisions) — a suggestion Ladakhi leaders have generally rejected as insufficient, insisting on the Sixth Schedule specifically rather than an alternative model.

Security and strategic considerations are frequently cited by analysts as a factor in the Centre's cautious approach, given Ladakh's sensitive dual-frontier position adjoining both the LoC (Pakistan) and LAC (China) — greater local autonomy over land and administrative matters is sometimes framed as carrying implications for national-security decision-making in this particularly sensitive border region (Chapter 12).

Economic and employment data have featured prominently in the public debate: Ladakh's youth unemployment has been cited in various reports as running significantly above the national average, a statistic invoked by movement leaders as evidence of the urgent need for the proposed Ladakh Public Service Commission and domicile-based job protections.

This remains a genuinely live, unresolved and actively evolving issue as of 2026 — candidates should present it factually, citing the timeline and both sides' stated positions, without asserting a predicted or already-achieved resolution.
Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2)/275(1)) currently covers only Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram; Ladakh's inclusion would require a constitutional amendment.
Twin demands: (1) full statehood (~30-member Assembly) and (2) Sixth Schedule protection — described by Ladakhi leaders as 'non-negotiable'.
Also sought: 2 separate Lok Sabha seats (Leh + Kargil, vs the current 1 combined seat) and a dedicated Ladakh Public Service Commission.

Sonam Wangchuk led the Sept-Oct 2024 'Delhi Chalo' padayatra and a March-May 2025 hunger strike; violent Leh protests on 24 Sept 2025 killed 4; Wangchuk detained under NSA 26 Sept 2025, released 14 March 2026.

High-Powered Committee (HPC, formed 2023) is the Centre's negotiating body; LAB and KDA are the joint Ladakhi civil-society platforms; a judicial inquiry commission was announced in October 2025 into the September violence.
